content: Castor oil is a vegetable oil derived from the seeds of the castor plant, Ricinus communis. Despite its name, the castor plant is not part of the bean family. Castor oil is a colorless to pale yellow liquid with little to no odor or taste. It has a boiling point of 313°C and a density of 961 kg/m³. Chemically, it is a triglyceride, with approximately 90% of its fatty acid chains composed of ricinoleic acid. Other significant components include oleic and linoleic acids. Ricinoleic acid, a monounsaturated fatty acid with 18 carbon atoms, is unique due to the presence of a hydroxyl functional group on its twelfth carbon. This hydroxyl group imparts unusual polarity to ricinoleic acid and castor oil, enabling chemical modifications that are not feasible with most other seed oils. This functional group also makes castor oil valuable as a chemical feedstock, which contributes to its higher market price compared to other seed oils. Castor oil and its derivatives are widely used in the production of soaps, lubricants, hydraulic and brake fluids, paints, dyes, coatings, inks, cold-resistant plastics, waxes, polishes, nylon, pharmaceuticals, and perfumes. The castor seed contains ricin, a toxic protein that is removed during cold pressing and filtering. However, harvesting castor beans poses health risks due to allergenic compounds on the plant's surface, which can cause permanent nerve damage. Workers in major producing countries like India, Brazil, and China often suffer harmful side effects from handling these plants. These health concerns, along with the toxicity of ricin as a byproduct of castor oil production, have driven efforts to find alternative sources of hydroxyl fatty acids or to genetically modify the castor plant to eliminate ricin synthesis. In the food industry, polyoxyethylated castor oil (e.g., Cremophor EL) is used as an emulsifier and stabilizer. Castor oil has also been employed as a mold inhibitor in food packaging. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies castor oil as generally recognized as safe and effective (GRASE) for over-the-counter use as a laxative, though it is not a preferred treatment for constipation. Undecylenic acid, a derivative of castor oil, is FDA-approved for treating skin disorders. Ricinoleic acid, the primary component of castor oil, exhibits anti-inflammatory properties. One study demonstrated that castor oil reduced pain more effectively than ultrasound gel or Vaseline during extracorporeal shock wave therapy. In modern pharmaceuticals, castor oil or its derivatives, such as Cremophor EL (a nonionic surfactant), are used as excipients in various drugs, including antifungal agents (e.g., miconazole), cancer chemotherapeutics (e.g., paclitaxel), immunosuppressants (e.g., cyclosporine), HIV protease inhibitors (e.g., nelfinavir mesylate), and antifungal triazoles (e.g., saperconazole). Castor oil is also included in topical formulations and vaginal gels. Historically, cold-pressed castor oil has been used in folk medicine for skin conditions, burns, sunburns, abrasions, and other ailments. It has been applied as a rub or pack for abdominal complaints, headaches, muscle pain, inflammatory conditions, and sinusitis. A castor oil pack involves soaking flannel in castor oil, applying it to the affected area, and placing a heat source on top. This remedy was popularized by Edgar Cayce, an American psychic, in the early to mid-1900s. Industrially, castor oil is utilized in transportation, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and manufacturing. It is found in adhesives, brake fluids, caulks, dyes, electrical dielectric fluids, humectants, hydraulic fluids, inks, lacquers, leather treatments, lubricants, machining oils, paints, pigments, polyurethane adhesives, refrigeration lubricants, rubbers, sealants, textiles, washing powders, and waxes. Castor oil's superior low-temperature viscosity and high-temperature lubrication properties make it suitable for use in jet, diesel, and race-car engines. However, it tends to form gums over time, limiting its use to engines that are frequently rebuilt, such as motorcycle race engines. Its biodegradability reduces environmental persistence compared to petroleum-based lubricants in the event of accidental release. The lubricant company Castrol derives its name from castor oil. Highly refined castor oil is sometimes used as a dielectric fluid in high-performance, high-voltage capacitors. It is also a raw material for producing chemicals like sebacic acid, undecylenic acid, and nylon-11. During Fascist Italy under Benito Mussolini, castor oil was infamously used as a tool of intimidation by the Blackshirts. Political dissidents were force-fed large quantities of castor oil, leading to severe diarrhea, dehydration, and often death. In some cases, gasoline was mixed with castor oil to ensure fatal outcomes. Mussolini's regime was said to be supported by the bludgeon and castor oil. In smaller doses, castor oil was used to intimidate civilians or soldiers feigning illness. Its purported healing properties were exaggerated, allowing its abuse to be masked as medical treatment. It took decades after Mussolini's death to dispel the myth of castor oil as a cure-all for various diseases and conditions. In modern Italian, the terms manganello (bludgeon) and olio di ricino (castor oil) retain strong political connotations. These terms are sometimes used to satirize authoritarian politicians or unpopular legislation but should be employed cautiously to avoid misinterpretation without proper context.
